To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

self-ratings and performance measures of EI are not strongly correlated, that men's MSCEITS scores, but not their self-ratings, predict their perceived social competence after controlling for personality, and that only the MSCEITS, but not self-report, predicted men's social competence during a real-time interaction.

self-ratings of emotional abilities were not correlated with performance measures of emotional abilities and that performance measures, but not self-reports, of emotional abilities correlated with real-time social functioning.
men's performance-based emotional intelligence scores, but not their self-ratings of their emotional intelligence, predicted their social competence in both a laboratory and a real-life setting.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the role of emotional intelligence (i.e., the abilities to accurately perceive, appraise, and express emotion; the abilities to access and/or generate feelings when they facilitate thought; the ability to understand emotions and emotional knowledge) in social functioning, as assessed both with self-report and performance-based measures.
the relationship of emotional abilities to social behavior.
how people's emotional abilities contribute to their social functioning.

the results of this study support the notion that EI is a multidimensional construct that can be assessed by self-report or performance measures.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the self-report measures of EI do not seem to be very good at measuring what the theory is about.
self-report measures of EI do not predict real-time social functioning.

emotional intelligence is a useful framework for examining the relation between emotional abilities and social behavior, but that it may be more useful to use performance measures of emotional abilities than self-ratings.
The main takeaway from our work is that
self-report measures of EI may not accurately capture emotional abilities and that the MSCEIT may be a better measure of EI.
the self-report measures of EI that are currently being used in the literature are likely not capturing the emotional abilities we think they are capturing.
the MSCEIT is a better predictor of social functioning than are self-ratings.
